title: Introduction to landscape metrics
text:
Preface
Understanding how organisms react to landscape and habitat structure is a key problem in ecology. It is thus important to know how to quantify and describe landscape patterns. This has motivated the development of hundreds of indices, especially in landscape ecology. Ecologists often used FRAGSTATS to compute such indices using land use or land cover (often abbreviated with LULC) gridded data sets. Unfortunately, FRAGSTATS is not an open source software, and its graphical user interface is not very adapted for reproducible workflows. Fortunately, it is now possible to compute many of these indices with R using the landscapemetrics package. The goal of this tutorial is to show how to get basic information on LULC rasters and how to compute the most common landscape ecology indices.
The first version of this tutorial was created for a course given at the Swiss Ornithological Institute in 2026. Researchers and students in ecology were the original audience but the whole material can be used by anybody who wants to learn more about how to perform these techniques.
None of this could have been written without the incredible work done by the R-spatial community. I’d especially like to thank all the software developers who created and are maintaining the R software, the R packages and the open-source libraries used in these packages! The content of this tutorial was also heavily inspired by the the landscapemetrics and motif official documentation. Thanks a lot to the authors.


Getting ready
You’ll need the following packages to run the examples in this book. You can use the following code to install them. All the required dependencies will be automatically installed.






Important



Please also update to the latest version of R, otherwise you may get packages that are not fully up-to-date.


install.packages("terra")
install.packages("sf")
install.packages("stars")
install.packages("landscapemetrics")
install.packages("motif")
The required data is available on the GitHub repository (https://github.com/jguelat/landscape-r). You’ll also find all the code needed to re-create the whole book.

title: 1  Raster data
text:
1.1 Raster data model
A raster data set is basically an image, which is the same as a grid of pixels. These pixels are often called cells. Most raster data sets you will encounter will have square (or maybe rectangular) cells with a constant size, also called resolution, and we will only focus on these in this tutorial. However don’t forget that other kind of grids, for example sheared or curvilinear ones, also exist. This is sometimes needed depending on the coordinate reference system used to store the data, or can be caused by some reprojections.
For this tutorial, we will focus on rasters containing discrete values. The content of each cell describes the dominant category of land use or land cover. However, rasters are also commonly used to store continuous values. Digital elevation models are a typical example of such data, each cell is used to store an elevation value. Continuous rasters can also be used to characterize landscapes and habitats, for example by storing the percentage of forest cover in each cell.
Raster data sets can sometimes have several bands. You can think of raster bands as different layers of the same grid, each layer containing a different information. This is mainly use for spectral data, for example the red, green and blue intensity values in an aerial picture; satellite imagery will have even more bands depending on the number of sensors. Multiband rasters are also often used to store environment variables that change through time (e.g. a temperature raster, with one band per day). Such rasters are often called datacubes.

title: 1  Raster data
text:
1.2 Raster data in R
We will use the terra package to work with raster data. This package has everything needed to import, analyse, visualize and export raster data sets. It is using the GDAL library for the import/export operations, which means it can open almost every raster data format. The terra functions will usually not import the full data sets in memory but only create a pointer to the data and then read smaller blocks of data successively. This allows working with very large rasters with a relatively small memory footprint. The terra package stores raster data inside objects called SpatRaster. The amount of functions available in the terra package is similar to typical GIS software.






ImportantRasters and R workspaces



It is important to remember that the standard terra objects only store a pointer to the data (actually, they hold a pointer to an underlying C++ object that lives in the memory of the R session). This means the actual data set will not be included if you save your session in an R workspace (.Rdata files). If you really want to include it in your workspace, you can use the wrap() function. Note that this is also needed if you want to pass terra objects over a connection that serializes, e.g. to a computer cluster. For more details on parallel computing using terra, check https://rspatial.org/pkg/10-parallel.html.


There is another famous R package to process raster data, the stars package. It is especially useful if you need to work with “irregular” rasters (sheared, curvilinear, etc.) or with complex datacubes. It is also tidyverse-friendly and the syntax is similar to the one used in sf (another R package used to work with GIS vector data). However the number of available functions is much lower than in terra. If you need to use both packages, it is fortunately easy to convert raster objects from terra to stars (using the function st_as_stars()), and the other way round (using the function rast()).

title: 1  Raster data
text:
1.3 Reading raster data
To import a raster data set using terra, we’re going to use the rast() function. It doesn’t matter if our raster is continuous, discrete, or contains several bands, the rast() function will create the correct terra object for us. Calling the object will display some basic information about the data set. However don’t forget that it’s only a pointer to the data set, the full raster will not be imported into memory.
The following raster is a typical land use/land cover dataset. It is an extract from the Swiss Land Use Statistics, provided by the Federal Statistical Office. Note that terra is not recognizing automatically that we’re processing a categorical raster. That’s why we need to use the as.factor() function.

landscape_sempach <- rast("data/landcover_4.tif")
landscape_sempach

class       : SpatRaster
size        : 151, 210, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 100, 100  (x, y)
extent      : 2644000, 2665000, 1212900, 1228000  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : CH1903+ / LV95 (EPSG:2056)
source      : landcover_4.tif
name        : landcover_4

landscape_sempach <- as.factor(landscape_sempach)
plot(landscape_sempach)








The values contained in a raster are always numeric, even for categorical data sets. Data providers must thus find a efficient way to encode the information they want to share using only numbers. With land use and land cover data sets, you’ll often find integer values used to represent categories. The values used in the Swiss Land Use Statistics are summarized in the following PDF document: https://statistik.admin.ch/en/asset/171190. You’ll find a more complete description of all the available categories there and there (only in German and French).
We’re currently using the least detailed data set with only 4 categories. In this data set, 1 is used for settlements and urban areas, 2 for agricultural areas, 3 for forests and 4 for unproductive areas. We can use the levels() function to add this information to our imported raster. After that we can easily query the categories using the cats() function.

df_levels <- data.frame(id = 1:4, cover = c("settlement", "agriculture", "forest", "unproductive"))
levels(landscape_sempach) <- df_levels
plot(landscape_sempach)







cats(landscape_sempach)

[[1]]
  id        cover
1  1   settlement
2  2  agriculture
3  3       forest
4  4 unproductive

title: 1  Raster data
text:
1.4 Writing raster data
Exporting a raster data set is really easy thanks to the writeRaster() function. The format will be automatically recognized based on the file name extension. Don’t worry too much about this, the GeoTIFF format is almost always the format we should use. If your raster object has several bands, all of them will be exported in the same GeoTIFF file. A lossless compression (LZW) will be applied by default.

writeRaster(landscape_sempach, "export/landscape_export.tif")

2.3 Raster binarization

landscape_sempach_layers <- segregate(landscape_sempach)
names(landscape_sempach_layers) <- c("settlement", "agriculture", "forest", "unproductive")

text:
2.4 Computing landcover proportions

pts <- vect("POINT(2657271 1219752)", crs = "EPSG:2056")
pts_buf <- buffer(pts, width = 5000)
plot(landscape_sempach)
plot(pts_buf, lwd = 3, border = "red", add = TRUE)







landcover_tbl <- extract(landscape_sempach, pts_buf, fun = table)
landcover_tbl

  ID        cover count
1  1   settlement  1002
2  1  agriculture  4524
3  1       forest  1218
4  1 unproductive  1073



landscape_sempach_agg <- aggregate(landscape_sempach_layers, 10, fun = function(i) {sum(i) / 100})
plot(landscape_sempach_agg)








Until now we saw examples of global, zonal and local analyses with raster data. Now we’re going to dive in the beautiful world of focal analyses. Note that people doing data science and mathematics will usually use the word convolution instead. Focal means that we’re not only considering the pixel value, but also the values of the neighboring pixels. The neighborhood is called kernel or moving window and is usually a square (like a 3x3 square, the focal pixel and its 8 neighbors) or a circle. Once the neighborhood is defined, we perform an aggregation of the pixel values (e.g. by summing or averaging) within the neighborhood and store the output as the new value for the focal cell, and then we move the window to the next pixel. The following figure shows a example using a 3x3 moving window and the minimum as the aggregating function.

Note that the output raster will usually be smaller than the original one (if the moving window is a \(m\)x\(n\) matrix, the output will have \((m-1)\) less rows and \((n-1)\) less columns). If you want a raster with the same size as the original, you’ll need to ignore the NA values, hence the window will be smaller in the margins of the raster.`
Focal analyses are really interesting to characterize the habitat of a site since you also get information about the neighboring areas. Using a discrete raster we can for example compute the number of pixels for each landcover classes in the neighborhood of each pixel. Note that the size of the moving window has to be an odd number.

landscape_sempach_focal <- focal(landscape_sempach_layers, 5, fun = "sum")
plot(landscape_sempach_focal)

title: 3  Landscape metrics
text:
3.1 Introduction
We first need to load the landscapemetrics package. This is the package we are going to use to compute landscape indices. Since the standard output of landscapemetrics is a tibble, we are also loading the dplyr package. This is not strictly needed since tibbles are also data frames, but the display will be a bit nicer.
library(landscapemetrics)
library(dplyr)
Since the computation time of some indices can be quite high on large landscapes, we are going to use a small simulated landscape provided by the package authors. It’s a 30x30 square landscape with 3 land cover categories.
landscape <- rast(landscape)
plot(landscape)
Before computing metrics, we first need to check that our input raster data is fulfilling all the requirements of landscapemetrics:
We thus check our simulated landscape. As a comparison, we also check the landscape we were using in the previous sections.
check_landscape(landscape)

Warning: Caution: Coordinate reference system not metric - Units of results
based on cellsizes and/or distances may be incorrect.


  layer crs units   class n_classes OK
1     1  NA    NA integer         3 ❓

check_landscape(landscape_sempach)

  layer       crs units   class n_classes OK
1     1 projected     m integer         4  ✔
We get a warning for the simulated data set since the CRS is not defined and landscapemetrics cannot know if the data is projected and/or using meters as a distance unit. To remove the warning, we will assign a projected CRS (we’ll use the one used in Switzerland) to the raster. This is not a problem here since we don’t care about the true location of this raster. However, in a real analysis, you should always check that your data has the appropriate CRS.
crs(landscape) <- "EPSG:2056"
check_landscape(landscape)

  layer       crs units   class n_classes OK
1     1 projected     m integer         3  ✔
You can use the list_lsm() function to get a list of all the metrics provided by landscapemetrics. Using the level and type arguments, it is also possible to get only the metrics for a specific level (patch, class or landscape) or a specific type of metrics.

title: 3  Landscape metrics
text:
The input raster is categorical (with a reasonable amount of categories)
Categories are encoded using integer values
The landscape uses a projected coordinate reference system (CRS)
The CRS uses meters as a distance unit

title: 3  Landscape metrics
text:
3.2 Patch metrics
A patch is an area of continuous land cover, and this continuity is defined by the numbers of connected neighbors. Most (maybe even all, I didn’t check) functions of landscapmetrics use 8 neighbors (queen’s case) but you can choose to use only 4 neighbors (rook’s case). This can have a strong influence on the number of delineated patches. The show_patches() function allows us to visualize the patches. Let’s use it with the 2 different settings.

show_patches(landscape, directions = 4, labels = TRUE)

$layer_1








show_patches(landscape, directions = 8, labels = TRUE)

$layer_1









When you compute a patch metric, you’ll get a value for every patch. This can be quite slow for large landscapes. As an example, let’s compute the area of each patch. This is done with the lsm_p_area() function.

res <- lsm_p_area(landscape)
res

# A tibble: 28 × 6
   layer level class    id metric  value
   <int> <chr> <int> <int> <chr>   <dbl>
 1     1 patch     1     1 area   0.0001
 2     1 patch     1     2 area   0.0005
 3     1 patch     1     3 area   0.0072
 4     1 patch     1     4 area   0.0001
 5     1 patch     1     5 area   0.0001
 6     1 patch     1     6 area   0.008 
 7     1 patch     1     7 area   0.0016
 8     1 patch     1     8 area   0.0003
 9     1 patch     1     9 area   0.0005
10     1 patch     2    10 area   0.0034
# ℹ 18 more rows


We get all the areas in hectares (check the help file if you want to know the units) and the output is stored in a tibble. We can thus use the usual data frame techniques to extract values, for example to get the IDs of all the patches with an area bigger than 0.005 ha.

res[res$class == 2 & res$value > 0.005, "id"]

# A tibble: 2 × 1
     id
  <int>
1    19
2    20


Some species don’t really like edge effects and thus avoid staying close to edges of a patch. In this case, the area of the patch is maybe not the best metric to use. Fortunately, there’s another metric that computes the core area of each patch.

res <- lsm_p_cai(landscape)
res

# A tibble: 28 × 6

   <int> <chr> <int> <int> <chr>  <dbl>

Let’s visualize the core areas of the patches for all three classes separately using the show_cores() function.

show_cores(landscape, class = "all")

$layer_1









Some functions, like lsm_p_cai() have additional arguments. For the core area index, we can specify the width of the edge using the edge_depth argument. The distance is specified in cell numbers.

res <- lsm_p_cai(landscape, edge_depth = 2)
res

10     1 patch     2    10 cai     2.94

show_cores(landscape, class = "all", edge_depth = 2)

$layer_1









It is sometimes useful to show the values of the patch metrics on a map. This can also help to understand the results of more complex metrics. The show_lsm() function creates such a map in which the value of each pixel is equal to the associated patch metric.

show_lsm(landscape, what = "lsm_p_area")

$layer_1









It is also possible to save this map as a SpatRaster object using the spatialize_lsm() function. The raster will be stored in a nested list. Only patch metrics are allowed.

res <- spatialize_lsm(landscape, what = "lsm_p_area")
res[[1]][[1]]

resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)

coord. ref. : CH1903+ / LV95 (EPSG:2056)
source(s)   : memory
name        :  value
min value   : 0.0001
max value   : 0.0159

One of the reason to start landscapemetrics was also to have a collection of metrics that are not included in FRAGSTATS. This vignette will highlight them and provide references for further reading on them. Information-theoretical framework can be applied to derive four metrics of landscape complexity: Marginal entropy [H(x)], Conditional entropy [H(y|x)], Joint entropy [H(x, y)], and Mutual information [I(y,x)]. https://r-spatialecology.github.io/landscapemetrics/articles/new_metrics.html
sample_lsm: percentage_inside: the size of the actual sampled landscape in %. It is not always 100% due to two reasons: (i) clipping raster cells using a buffer not directly intersecting a raster cell center lead to inaccuracies and (ii) sample plots can exceed the landscape boundary.

title: 4  More help
text:
If you need a more general introduction to GIS and spatial data processing with R, check my tutorial available at https://jguelat.github.io/spatial-r/. Actually, I’m planning to include the material on landscape metrics in the main tutorial (after some polishing). The book Geocomputation with R is absolutely amazing and available for free (legally) on the web: https://r.geocompx.org. The book Spatial Data Science also provides some advanced information on spatial data: https://r-spatial.org/book/.
The FRAGSTATS documentation provides plenty of information on several landscape ecology concepts and a complete description of all the available metrics: https://www.fragstats.org/index.php/documentation.
If you need more help, documentation or code examples for landscapemetrics, check its website (https://r-spatialecology.github.io/landscapemetrics/) and the associated paper https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.04617. Paige Wirth, from the SILVIS Lab (University of Wisconsin–Madison), has a great video tutorial on landscape ecology indices and landscapemetrics: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WdqLMaCesjM.
If you like motif, the website has additional examples. The associated paper has a lot of information, too: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-020-01135-0.
Jakub Nowosad, one the developers of landscapemetrics and the main developer of motif, wrote some interesting blog posts on this topic: https://jakubnowosad.com/posts.html.
